prompt: In an alkyl chloride such as CH3CH2Cl, how is the carbon bonded to chlorine polarized?

choices.text: δ+, because chlorine is more electronegative than carbon
δ−, because chlorine is more electronegative than carbon
choices.why: The more electronegative atom pulls the bonding electrons toward itself, so chlorine is δ− and carbon is left δ+.

choices.text: δ−, because carbon is more electronegative than chlorine
choices.why: Chlorine is more electronegative than carbon, as are oxygen, nitrogen, and fluorine.

choices.text: Not polarized, because C–Cl bonds are nonpolar
choices.why: Table 6.3.1 shows the alkyl halide C–X bond as polar, with carbon δ+ and the halogen δ−.

explanation: Elements such as oxygen, nitrogen, fluorine, and chlorine are more electronegative than carbon, so a carbon atom bonded to one of these atoms has a partial positive charge (δ+).

prompt: How is the carbon atom in methyllithium, CH3Li, polarized?

choices.text: δ−, because lithium is less electronegative than carbon
δ+, because carbon is always positively polarized
choices.why: Carbon is positively polarized in most functional groups, but not when bonded to a metal.

choices.text: δ+, because lithium is more electronegative than carbon
choices.why: Metals are less electronegative than carbon, so the bonding electrons are pulled toward carbon.

choices.text: Not polarized, because carbon and lithium have the same electronegativity
choices.why: They differ: lithium is a metal and less electronegative, which makes the carbon electron-rich.

explanation: Metals are less electronegative than carbon, so a carbon atom bonded to a metal has a partial negative charge (δ−). The electrostatic potential map of methyllithium shows its carbon as electron-rich (red).

prompt: In which of these functional groups from Table 6.3.1 is the carbon negatively polarized?

choices.text: A Grignard reagent, R–MgBr
A ketone, with a C=O group
choices.why: The carbonyl carbon is δ+ and the oxygen δ−.

choices.text: A thiol, R–SH
choices.why: Table 6.3.1 shows the carbon of a thiol as δ+ and the sulfur as δ−.

choices.text: A nitrile, R–C≡N
choices.why: The nitrile carbon is δ+ and the nitrogen δ−.

explanation: In Table 6.3.1, carbon is always positively polarized except when bonded to a metal. In a Grignard reagent the carbon is bonded to magnesium, so the carbon is δ− and the magnesium δ+.

prompt: How does Table 6.3.1 describe the C=C bond of an alkene?

choices.text: Symmetrical and nonpolar
Polar, with one carbon δ+ and the other δ−
choices.why: Both atoms are carbon, so there is no electronegativity difference to polarize the bond.

choices.text: Polar, with both carbons δ+
choices.why: Carbons are δ+ when bonded to more electronegative atoms; two carbons bonded to each other share electrons equally.

choices.text: Polar, with both carbons δ−
choices.why: Carbons are δ− only when bonded to a metal; an alkene's C=C bond is nonpolar.

explanation: Table 6.3.1 labels the alkene C=C as symmetrical and nonpolar: the two bonded atoms are both carbon, so there is no difference in electronegativity.

prompt: What happens to the carbon of methanol, CH3OH, when an acid protonates the oxygen?

choices.text: It becomes much more electron-poor, because the full positive charge on oxygen pulls the C–O electrons more strongly
It becomes electron-rich, because it gains the proton's charge
choices.why: The H^+ adds to oxygen, not carbon, and the resulting positive oxygen pulls electrons away from carbon.

choices.text: Nothing changes, because the proton adds to oxygen, not carbon
choices.why: The full positive charge on oxygen strongly attracts the C–O electrons, so the carbon is affected.

choices.text: The C–O bond becomes nonpolar
choices.why: Protonation increases the bond's polarity rather than removing it.

explanation: In neutral methanol the carbon is somewhat electron-poor. On protonation, a full positive charge on oxygen attracts the electrons in the C–O bond much more strongly and makes the carbon much more electron-poor.

prompt: What is the polarizability of an atom?

choices.text: A measure of how its electron distribution responds to a changing external electrical influence
A measure of how strongly it attracts the electrons in a bond
choices.why: That is electronegativity, which causes bond polarity. Polarizability is a different property.

choices.text: The partial charge it carries in a bond
choices.why: The partial charge (δ+ or δ−) describes polarity. Polarizability is how easily the electron cloud is distorted.

choices.text: Its tendency to break bonds symmetrically
choices.why: Symmetrical bond-breaking describes radical reactions, not polarizability.

explanation: As the electric field around an atom changes because of interactions with solvent or other polar molecules nearby, the electron distribution around that atom also changes. The measure of this response to an external electrical influence is called the polarizability of the atom.

prompt: Which atom is more polarizable, and why?

choices.text: Iodine more than chlorine, because larger atoms with loosely held electrons are more polarizable
Chlorine more than iodine, because chlorine is more electronegative
choices.why: Electronegativity governs polarity, not polarizability. Smaller atoms with tightly held electrons are less polarizable.

choices.text: Oxygen more than sulfur, because oxygen is smaller
choices.why: Smaller atoms with fewer, tightly held electrons are less polarizable; sulfur is more polarizable than oxygen.

choices.text: Chlorine and iodine equally, because they are in the same group
choices.why: Being in the same group doesn't make them equal: iodine is larger, with more loosely held electrons.

explanation: Larger atoms with more loosely held electrons are more polarizable, and smaller atoms with fewer, tightly held electrons are less polarizable. Thus sulfur is more polarizable than oxygen, and iodine is more polarizable than chlorine.

prompt: C–S and C–I bonds are nearly nonpolar according to electronegativity values. How do they usually react?

choices.text: As if they were polar, because sulfur and iodine are highly polarizable
As nonpolar bonds, because electronegativity alone decides reactivity
choices.why: Electronegativity isn't the whole story; the high polarizability of S and I makes these bonds behave as polar.

choices.text: With carbon as the electron-rich end
choices.why: These bonds react with carbon δ+ and the sulfur or iodine δ−.

choices.text: Only by radical reactions
choices.why: Because of polarizability, they usually react as polar bonds, with carbon δ+ and S or I δ−.

explanation: The higher polarizability of sulfur and iodine means that carbon–sulfur and carbon–iodine bonds, although nonpolar according to electronegativity values, nevertheless usually react as if they were polar, with carbon δ+ and S or I δ−.

prompt: What is the fundamental characteristic of all polar organic reactions?

choices.text: Electron-rich sites react with electron-poor sites
Electron-rich sites react with other electron-rich sites
choices.why: Like charges repel. Because unlike charges attract, electron-rich sites react with electron-poor ones.

choices.text: Each bond breaks with one electron going to each atom
choices.why: That is symmetrical (homolytic) bond-breaking, found in radical reactions.

choices.text: Only charged ions can react
choices.why: Neutral molecules react too, through their polarized δ+ and δ− sites.

explanation: Because unlike charges attract, the fundamental characteristic of all polar organic reactions is that electron-rich sites react with electron-poor sites.

prompt: In a polar reaction, how is a bond broken?

choices.text: One atom leaves with both electrons from the former bond
Each atom keeps one electron from the former bond
choices.why: That symmetrical breaking happens in radical reactions; polar bond-breaking is unsymmetrical.

choices.text: An electron-poor atom donates a pair of electrons
choices.why: Electron-poor atoms accept pairs. Bonds are made when an electron-rich atom donates a pair.

choices.text: Both electrons are released from the molecule
choices.why: The electrons are not lost; they leave with one of the two atoms.

explanation: Bonds are made when an electron-rich atom donates a pair of electrons to an electron-poor atom, and bonds are broken when one atom leaves with both electrons from the former bond.

prompt: In a polar reaction, which way does the curved, full-headed arrow point?

choices.text: From the electron pair of the nucleophile to the electrophile
From the electrophile to the nucleophile
choices.why: Curved arrows show where electrons move, and electrons move from the electron-rich nucleophile to the electron-poor electrophile.

choices.text: From the positive atom toward the negative atom
choices.why: That would show electrons coming from the electron-poor site. Arrows start at the electron-rich site.

choices.text: It is drawn as a fishhook arrow from each reactant
choices.why: Fishhook arrows show one electron moving, as in radical reactions. Polar reactions move pairs, shown with full-headed arrows.

explanation: As in Section 2.11, the movement of an electron pair during a polar reaction is shown with a curved, full-headed arrow, pointing from the lone pair on the electron-rich nucleophile to the electron-poor electrophile.

prompt: What is a nucleophile?

choices.text: A substance with an electron-rich atom that forms a bond by donating a pair of electrons to an electron-poor atom
A substance with an electron-poor atom that forms a bond by accepting a pair of electrons
choices.why: That is an electrophile.

choices.text: A substance that must carry a negative charge
choices.why: Nucleophiles can be neutral or negatively charged; ammonia and water are neutral nucleophiles.

choices.text: A substance attracted to other electron-rich atoms
choices.why: "Nucleus-loving" means attracted to positive charge, so nucleophiles seek electron-poor atoms.

explanation: A nucleophile is "nucleus-loving" (a nucleus is positively charged). It has a negatively polarized, electron-rich atom and can form a bond by donating a pair of electrons to a positively polarized, electron-poor atom.

prompt: What is an electrophile?

choices.text: A substance with a positively polarized, electron-poor atom that forms a bond by accepting a pair of electrons from a nucleophile
A substance that forms a bond by donating a pair of electrons
choices.why: Donating an electron pair is what a nucleophile does.

choices.text: A substance that must carry a positive charge
choices.why: Electrophiles can be neutral or positively charged; alkyl halides and carbonyl compounds are neutral electrophiles.

choices.text: A substance with an unpaired electron
choices.why: A species with an unpaired electron is a radical. Electrophiles accept electron pairs in polar reactions.

explanation: An electrophile is "electron-loving." It has a positively polarized, electron-poor atom and can form a bond by accepting a pair of electrons from a nucleophile. Acids (H^+ donors), alkyl halides, and carbonyl compounds are examples (Figure 6.2).

prompt: How many electrons does a nucleophile donate to form a new bond to an electrophile?
explanation: A nucleophile forms a bond by donating a pair of electrons (two electrons) to a positively polarized, electron-poor atom.

prompt: Which of these species is most likely to behave as a nucleophile?

choices.text: CH3O^−
H3O^+
choices.why: H3O^+ is positively charged and an H^+ donor, so it is an electrophile (Figure 6.2).

choices.text: CH3CH2Br
choices.why: Alkyl halides have a δ+ carbon and are electrophiles.
A positively charged species is likely to be an electrophile, not an electron-pair donor.

explanation: A nucleophile has an electron-rich site, either because it is negatively charged or because it has an atom with a lone pair. The methoxide ion, CH3O^−, is negatively charged, so it is likely to be a nucleophile.

prompt: Which of these species is most likely to behave as an electrophile?

choices.text: CH3CH2I
NH3
choices.why: Ammonia has a lone pair on nitrogen and is one of the text's examples of a nucleophile.

choices.text: Br^−
choices.why: A negatively charged ion is electron-rich and likely to be a nucleophile, like chloride ion.

choices.text: HO^−
choices.why: Hydroxide ion is negatively charged and is a nucleophile.

explanation: An electrophile has an electron-poor site. Alkyl halides are electrophiles: the carbon bonded to the halogen is positively polarized, and even the C–I bond reacts as polar because iodine is highly polarizable.

prompt: When does water act as an electrophile rather than a nucleophile?

choices.text: When it donates H^+
When it donates a nonbonding pair of electrons
choices.why: Donating an electron pair is how water acts as a nucleophile.

choices.text: Never; water is always a nucleophile
choices.why: Neutral compounds can often react either way. Water acts as an electrophile when it donates H^+.

choices.text: When it accepts H^+ on oxygen
choices.why: Accepting H^+ uses an oxygen lone pair, which is nucleophilic (base) behavior.

explanation: Neutral compounds can often react as either nucleophiles or electrophiles. Water acts as an electrophile when it donates H^+ but acts as a nucleophile when it donates a nonbonding pair of electrons.

prompt: A carbonyl compound can act as either an electrophile or a nucleophile. Which site is involved in each case?

choices.text: Electrophile at the positively polarized carbon; nucleophile at the negatively polarized oxygen
Electrophile at the oxygen; nucleophile at the carbon
choices.why: That is backward: the C=O carbon is δ+ (electron-poor) and the oxygen δ− (electron-rich).

choices.text: Both at the carbon
choices.why: The δ+ carbon is the electrophilic site; the nucleophilic site is the δ− oxygen with its lone pairs.

choices.text: Both at the oxygen
choices.why: The oxygen is electron-rich, so it reacts as a nucleophile; the electrophilic site is the δ+ carbon.

explanation: If a neutral compound has an electron-rich nucleophilic site, it must also have an electron-poor electrophilic site. A carbonyl compound acts as an electrophile at its positively polarized carbon and as a nucleophile at its negatively polarized oxygen.

prompt: How do nucleophiles and electrophiles correspond to Lewis acids and bases?

choices.text: Lewis bases behave as nucleophiles, and Lewis acids behave as electrophiles
Lewis acids behave as nucleophiles, and Lewis bases behave as electrophiles
choices.why: Lewis acids accept electron pairs, like electrophiles; Lewis bases donate them, like nucleophiles.

choices.text: There is no relationship between the two sets of terms
choices.why: There is a correlation, which is why much of organic chemistry is explainable in terms of acid–base reactions.

choices.text: Both Lewis acids and Lewis bases are nucleophiles
choices.why: Only electron donors (Lewis bases) behave as nucleophiles; electron acceptors (Lewis acids) are electrophiles.

explanation: Lewis bases are electron donors and behave as nucleophiles, whereas Lewis acids are electron acceptors and behave as electrophiles (Section 2.11). Thus much of organic chemistry is explainable in terms of acid–base reactions.

prompt: What is the main difference between the terms acid/base and electrophile/nucleophile?

choices.text: Acid and base are used in all fields of chemistry, while electrophile and nucleophile are used mainly in organic chemistry when carbon bonding is involved
Electrophiles accept electron pairs, but Lewis acids donate them
choices.why: Lewis acids also accept electron pairs; the difference is in usage, not in the electron flow.

choices.text: Nucleophile and electrophile apply only to charged species
choices.why: Many nucleophiles and electrophiles are neutral, such as water and alkyl halides.

choices.text: Acid and base apply only to reactions in water
choices.why: The Lewis definitions are not limited to water. The distinction is that nucleophile and electrophile are used mainly when carbon bonding is involved.

explanation: The main difference is that the words acid and base are used broadly in all fields of chemistry, while the words nucleophile and electrophile are used primarily in organic chemistry when carbon bonding is involved.
